The lowest-level entry point bypasses all orchestration and gives you exactly the two classes from the diagram:

from pyannote.audio import Model
from pyannote.audio.core.inference import Inference

# a pretrained speech segmentation checkpoint, downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub
model = Model.from_pretrained("pyannote/segmentation-3.0")

# sliding-window inference over any file Inference can decode
inference = Inference(model)
scores = inference("meeting.wav")

Model.from_pretrained resolves the checkpoint on the Hub through the asset helper at download_from_hf_hub, L44, restores the architecture, and returns a LightningModule you can also keep training. Inference then handles windowing and aggregation; the result is frame-wise speaker probabilities indexed by time, ready for thresholding with the Binarize, L204 utility or any post-processing you prefer.

For the full “who spoke when” story, the library ships a high-level diarization orchestration module that chains a segmentation model, an embedding extractor and a clustering step into one callable. That module lives outside the trainable core diagrammed above — it consumes Model instances and Inference output rather than defining them — which is exactly why the core stays testable: the composition layer can change without touching how anything is trained. If you have used WhisperX for transcription alignment, you have already met this composition: it reuses pyannote’s diarization entry point for its speaker labels. And if your product needs text-to-speech instead of speaker analysis, Piper covers the synthesis side of the same audio stack.

Training your own model follows the same shape. Pick an architecture, wrap it in a task with a pyannote.database protocol, and hand both to the Lightning trainer. The training_step, L402 implementation in the diarization task shows the whole recipe in one place: sample a chunk, decode its targets with the powerset transform, compute the multi-task loss, and log the metric family from OptimalDiarizationErrorRate, L273 that finds the best operating threshold on validation data.

Honest Limits

The framework tax is real. Training tasks require pyannote.database protocol objects, which means assembling a database collection with exact file paths and annotations before the first epoch runs. For datasets with messy folder layouts this is the most time-consuming part of the setup — more so than the model code itself. The reward is reproducibility, but you pay for it up front.

Multi-speaker overlap remains genuinely hard. The powerset decoding trick makes overlap learnable by a standard classification head, but with more than a handful of concurrent speakers the class count grows quickly, and diarization quality still degrades on real meeting audio with crosstalk, distant microphones and reverberant rooms. The pretrained checkpoints are strong on broadcast-style data and noticeably weaker elsewhere.

The metric can flatter you. DER variants that search for an optimal threshold on the validation set, like the ones at OptimalDiarizationErrorRate, L273, are convenient for model selection but optimistic relative to a fixed-threshold deployment; the raw DiarizationErrorRate, L34 with a fixed decision threshold is the conservative number to quote.

Finally, the abstractions cut both ways. Because architectures subclass Model and tasks subclass Task, you can replace any piece in isolation — but you inherit Lightning’s conventions everywhere: device handling, checkpoint formats, callback timing and data-loader semantics are all Lightning’s, not yours. The Inference class also processes files window by window, which is memory-friendly but not the fastest path if you only need one short clip; for speech-command or keyword-spotting workloads a lighter toolkit may serve you better than a diarization framework.

None of these limits are accidents. They are the visible edges of a design that treats diarization, VAD and embedding extraction as one learning problem with three heads — and reading the source makes that design, its trade-offs and its extension points all explicit.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the pyannote.audio source on GitHub: how Model, Task, Audio and Inference fit together with PyanNet-style architectures, ArcFace embeddings and TorchMetrics to train speaker diarization, VAD and speaker embedding models.

entry.title: Swin Transformer: A Source Tour of Microsoft’s Hierarchical Vision Backbone

link.title: Swin Transformer: A Source Tour of Microsoft’s Hierarchical Vision Backbone

entry.content:
When the Swin Transformer landed in 2021, most vision transformers were still computing attention over every pair of tokens in the image — quadratic cost, single-scale feature maps, and an awkward fit for dense prediction tasks that expect pyramid-shaped backbones. Microsoft’s answer, written by Ze Liu and collaborators, was to restrict self-attention to small local windows and then shift those windows by half their size every other block, so information still flows across the whole image. The result became the default backbone for a generation of detection and segmentation systems, including the Detectron2 ecosystem, and its hierarchical four-stage design still shows up in modern architectures.

What makes this repository especially worth reading is that the ideas map onto the code with almost no abstraction layer. There is one file, models/swin_transformer.py, that contains the entire model: patch embedding, windowed attention, shifted-window masking, patch merging, and the classification head. Around it sit a thin yacs-based config system, a data loading module built on PyTorch and timm primitives, and a distributed training entry that was clearly written to run on 8-GPU ImageNet boxes. Reading it top to bottom teaches you not just Swin, but how production vision training repos were structured in that era.

In this tour we walk the source the way a maintainer would: the model file first, then the shifted-window mechanics, the downsampling stage, the checkpoint loading quirks, and finally the training entry. Two diagrams generated from the actual repository tree anchor the discussion.

Overview of the repo: main.py orchestrates config, data, optimizer, and scheduler, while models/build.py instantiates the SwinTransformer backbone from models/swin_transformer.py.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SwinTransformer, L485 — the top-level nn.Module that assembles patch embedding, four stages, final norm, and the linear head.
  • PatchEmbed, L437 — a strided 4×4 Conv2d that chops the image into non-overlapping patches and flattens them into tokens.
  • BasicLayer, L364 — one stage of the hierarchy: a stack of blocks followed by optional downsampling.
  • SwinTransformerBlock, L175 — the workhorse block that alternates regular and shifted window attention around an MLP.
  • WindowAttention, L77 — multi-head self-attention confined to an M×M window, with a learned relative position bias table.
  • PatchMerging, L315 — the resolution-halving layer that gives Swin its pyramid shape.
  • build_model, L15 — a config-driven dispatcher that also knows about Swin-V2, Swin-MoE, and Swin-MLP variants.
  • main, L90 — the distributed training and evaluation entry that wires everything together.
  • load_pretrained, L45 — the fine-tuning loader that repairs mismatched weights, including bicubic resizing of the bias tables.

Why Windows Instead of Global Attention

The motivating trade-off is cost. Global self-attention over H×W/16 tokens scales quadratically with image size, which is brutal for detection backbones that must process 800×1333 feature maps. Swin instead partitions the feature map into non-overlapping windows of default size M=7 and attends only within each window, making the cost linear in the number of tokens. The helper functions window_partition, L45 and window_reverse, L60 are just view/permute reshapes that move between (B, H, W, C) and a batch of (num_windows*B, M, M, C) tensors — no fancy kernels required for the baseline path.

The catch is that attention confined to fixed windows has no communication across window borders. Swin’s fix is the shifted window scheme: even-numbered blocks use regular windows (W-MSA), odd-numbered blocks shift the feature map by ⌊M/2⌋ pixels along both axes first. After the shift, windows straddle the boundaries of the previous layer’s windows, so tokens from different regions end up in the same attention group. You can see this in SwinTransformerBlock.forward at the cyclic shift, L260, where torch.roll moves the feature map, and in BasicLayer’s construction at L397, which alternates shift_size=0 with shift_size=window_size//2 across blocks.

Rolling creates one artifact: a window that wraps around the image edge contains tokens that are not actually spatial neighbors. Rather than wasting compute on those connections, the block precomputes an attention mask in its constructor (register_buffer("attn_mask", ...), L245) that adds −100 to cross-region attention logits, effectively zeroing them after softmax. The mask is a buffer, not a parameter, so it is recomputed per resolution and — importantly — deleted by the checkpoint loader rather than restored from disk.

The Anatomy of a Shifted Window Block

Each SwinTransformerBlock follows the classic pre-norm transformer recipe with two sublayers. The first applies LayerNorm, optionally rolls the feature map, partitions windows, and calls WindowAttention, L77. The second is a GELU MLP with a 4× expansion, implemented in the modest Mlp, L26 class. Both sublayers are wrapped in residual connections with stochastic-depth (DropPath) regularization.

Inside WindowAttention, three details deserve attention. First, the QKV projection is a single nn.Linear(dim, dim*3) followed by a reshape into heads — standard, but note the explicit q * self.scale before the matmul, since this code predates PyTorch’s fused scaled_dot_product_attention. Second, the attention logits get a learned bias added: the relative_position_bias_table, L101 is a (2M−1)² × num_heads parameter table, and a precomputed relative_position_index buffer maps each of the M²×M² token pairs inside a window to one row of that table. This relative bias is what lets the model know where tokens sit within their window without any absolute positional embedding. Third, the block exposes no_weight_decay_keywords at L585 so the optimizer excludes this table from weight decay — a small but consequential training detail handled in build_optimizer, L19.

The optimizer code itself is worth a skim. set_weight_decay, L59 splits parameters into decay/no-decay groups based on parameter shape (1-D tensors like norms get zero decay) and the skip lists above. On the schedule side, build_scheduler, L16 wraps timm’s cosine scheduler with a linear warmup, and the repo also ships a homegrown LinearLRScheduler, L66 for recipes that prefer linear decay. The entry point then linearly scales the learning rate with total batch size at main.py L327, a convention from the large-batch ImageNet training era.

PatchMerging and the Four-Stage Hierarchy

Where ViT keeps one resolution throughout, Swin builds a pyramid that CNN-based detectors expect: resolutions H/4, H/8, H/16, H/32 with channel widths doubling at each stage. The glue between stages is PatchMerging. Its forward pass at PatchMerging.forward, L331 slices the feature map into even/odd rows and columns, concatenates the four neighbors along the channel dimension (2C becomes 4C), applies LayerNorm, and then a linear layer without bias that projects 4C back down to 2C. Resolution halves, width doubles — exactly the role a strided convolution plays in ResNet.

The SwinTransformer constructor at L529 wires this up by instantiating one BasicLayer per stage, passing downsample=PatchMerging for every stage except the last. Each BasicLayer builds depths[i] blocks with alternating shift sizes, and optionally wraps each block in gradient checkpointing when use_checkpoint is set — a memory saver that matters for the 384-resolution and Swin-L configurations. After the final stage, forward_features, L588 applies a final LayerNorm, average-pools over tokens, and hands the feature vector to the classification head. Because every piece is a plain module with a flops() method, the repo reports GFLOPs for any configuration at startup.

Checkpoint Loading and Relative Position Remapping

The subtlety in this repo is that several “parameters” of a Swin model are actually resolution-dependent buffers: relative_position_index, attn_mask, and the size of relative_position_bias_table itself. That means a checkpoint trained at 224×224 cannot be loaded verbatim into a 384×384 model. The fine-tuning loader load_pretrained, L45 handles this with surgical string matching over state-dict keys.

First it deletes all relative_position_index and attn_mask entries, since those are always re-initialized from the new model’s geometry (L51 onward). Then, for each relative_position_bias_table whose row count changed, it bicubically interpolates the pretrained table to the new (2M−1)² size — the remap logic lives at L66. Finally, if the classifier head mismatches, it does something clever for the ImageNet-22K → 1K transfer: rather than re-initializing, it reads data/map22kto1k.txt, a fixed 21841→1000 index map, and slices the pretrained head rows accordingly (L111). That one file explains how the 22K-pretrained checkpoints reach their published 1K accuracies out of the box. The resume path, load_checkpoint, L18, is the ordinary strict-shape restore of model, optimizer, scheduler, and AMP scaler for interrupted runs.

From Install to Your First Model

The get_started guide targets CUDA 10.2-era environments and pins old versions deliberately — the code relies on timm internals that changed after 0.4.12. The setup sequence is:

conda create -n swin python=3.7 -y
conda activate swin
conda install pytorch==1.8.0 torchvision==0.9.0 cudatoolkit=10.2 -c pytorch
pip install timm==0.4.12
pip install opencv-python==4.4.0.46 termcolor==1.1.0 yacs==0.1.8 pyyaml scipy

The repo never grew a requirements.txt on its main branch; the guide pins each dependency explicitly instead, so treat those five lines as the source of truth. With a torch build of your choosing, the fastest way to touch the model is a single-GPU evaluation of the Swin-B checkpoint:

python -m torch.distributed.launch --nproc_per_node 1 --master_port 12345 main.py --eval \
  --cfg configs/swin/swin_base_patch4_window7_224.yaml \
  --resume swin_base_patch4_window7_224.pth --data-path <imagenet-path>

Training uses the same entry with --cfg configs/swin/swin_tiny_patch4_window7_224.yaml and --nproc_per_node 8, as documented in the guide’s ImageNet-1K section. Under the hood, parse_option, L36 merges CLI flags into the yacs defaults via get_config, L352, which in turn loads the chosen YAML through _update_config_from_file, L268. Data flows through build_loader, L44, which selects between torchvision-style folders, a cached in-memory variant, and the ImageNet-22K archive reader in data/, then attaches mixup/CutMix from the timm data module. One epoch of the training loop, train_one_epoch, L174, uses AMP mixed precision through a wrapped grad scaler and logs lr, loss, grad norm, and memory each step; validate, L235 reports top-1/top-5 on the val split. Note that torch.distributed.launch is deprecated in modern PyTorch — with torch 2.x the code switches to reading LOCAL_RANK from the environment, per the comment at main.py L70.

The detailed view adds the attention internals, data loading, optimizer/scheduler construction, and the checkpoint utilities in utils.py.

Honest Limits

Treat this repository as a paper-replica research artifact from 2021–2022, not a maintained library. It is effectively archived: the last significant updates landed in mid-2022. The training recipes assume serious hardware — the published ImageNet numbers come from 8× V100-class GPUs, and the ImageNet-22K pre-training runs are well beyond a single workstation, even with gradient checkpointing and --accumulation-steps. The dependency pins are the other friction point: timm==0.4.12 is ancient, and importing the model with current timm versions breaks on the timm.models.layers import path (modern timm moved it to timm.layers). If you want Swin weights in a maintained stack, timm re-implements every Swin variant with its own builder and pretrain tags, and the Hugging Face torchvision releases include shifted-window backbones for detection work.

Architecturally, Swin has been superseded twice over: the same group’s Swin-V2 (also in this repo, under models/swin_transformer_v2.py) replaced the bias table with a log-spaced coordinate function to handle larger windows, and the field has since moved to hybrid and plain ViT designs. None of this changes the historical verdict: Swin’s windowed hierarchical design made transformers practical as drop-in CNN replacements, and this codebase remains the clearest executable specification of that idea.
entry.summary: Walk through the Swin source: shifted-window self-attention with relative position bias, patch merging downsampling, checkpoint weight remapping, and the training entry.

entry.title: TensorFlow Serving: A Source Tour of Google’s Model Server

link.title: TensorFlow Serving: A Source Tour of Google’s Model Server

entry.content:
TensorFlow Serving is Google’s open-source model server: the piece of infrastructure that takes a trained TensorFlow model off a researcher’s laptop and makes it answer real network traffic, reliably, at low latency. You export a SavedModel into a versioned directory, point the server at the parent folder, and it discovers every numbered version, loads the newest one, swaps versions atomically while old requests drain, and answers Predict, Classify, Regress, and GetModelMetadata calls over both gRPC and an HTTP/REST endpoint. It ships as a single prebuilt binary, tensorflow_model_server, published through apt packages and Docker images, and it has quietly run a large share of Google’s internal inference traffic for years.

Why bother reading its source at all? Because this is one of the few production-grade serving systems written almost entirely in C++, and the code is organized around a small set of interfaces — Source, SourceAdapter, Loader, Manager — that compose into a genuinely elegant component model. Once you see how those pieces snap together, you understand not just this server but the general anatomy of every model server you will ever touch. It also makes a sharp contrast with the Python-centric stacks we have covered before, like TorchServe, and with the multi-framework Triton Server, both of which lean on Python or backend-specific runtimes where TensorFlow Serving compiles everything down to one C++ process.

This post is a source tour, not a tutorial. Every symbol below links to a real file and line on the master branch, and the two architecture diagrams were generated directly from the actual repository tree. We will follow the server from main() all the way to a batched session execution, then close with the practical bits — installation, first model, and the limits you will hit in production.

What the Server Must Solve

Before diving into files, it helps to enumerate the problems a model server has to solve, because every directory in the repository maps to one of them. First, discovery: new model versions appear on disk (or on GCS or S3) while the server is running, and something must notice. Second, versioning policy: when version 7 shows up while version 6 still serves traffic, the server needs rules for when to load 7, when to unload 6, and what to do if loading 7 fails. Third, loading itself: a SavedModel must be deserialized into a session with its graph, signature definitions, and variables, and that load can take minutes for large models. Fourth, efficiency: single requests are wasteful for GPUs, so the server can coalesce concurrent requests into batches. Fifth, presentation: gRPC, REST, health checks, and monitoring endpoints all need to expose the same underlying manager state.

The repository layout mirrors this list almost exactly. tensorflow_serving/sources/ contains things that watch the outside world, tensorflow_serving/core/ contains the version-management machinery, tensorflow_serving/servables/tensorflow/ knows how to turn a SavedModel into something callable, tensorflow_serving/batching/ implements request coalescing, and tensorflow_serving/model_servers/ glues everything into the binary you actually run. That symmetry between problem and directory is the first sign of a well-factored codebase, and it is what makes the diagrams below readable.

The TensorFlow Serving stack, from the command-line entry point through model discovery, version management, and the batched request path.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L82 is where the binary starts. It declares roughly forty command-line flags — port, model_base_path, batching parameters, session parallelism — into an Options struct and hands it to the server builder at main, L342.
  • Server::BuildAndStart, L182 creates the ServerCore, registers the gRPC services, optionally starts the REST frontend, and then blocks in WaitForTermination, L464 until shutdown.
  • ServerCore::Create, L260 is the true orchestrator. Its Initialize, L306 method builds the three moving parts — source, adapters, manager — and WaitUntilModelsAvailable, L328 keeps startup blocked until every configured model is actually servable.
  • On the discovery side, FileSystemStoragePathSource::Create, L373 starts a polling thread; PollFileSystemForConfig, L329 scans each base path for numerically named subdirectories, and PollFileSystemAndInvokeCallback, L444 pushes the result as aspired versions.
  • SavedModelBundleSourceAdapter::Create, L36 builds the adapter that converts each aspired storage path into a loadable servable, wiring the adapter chain the core requested in CreateAdapters, L728.
  • SavedModelBundleFactory::CreateSavedModelBundle, L116 does the heavy lifting: it loads the meta-graph, session, and signature map, then optionally replays recorded traffic via RunSavedModelWarmup, L82 so the first real request is not slow.
  • On the management side, ServerCore::CreateAspiredVersionsManager, L785 builds the AspiredVersionsManager, L85, the state machine that owns every loaded and loading servable in the process.
  • That manager orders candidates with a pluggable policy — the model server default is AvailabilityPreservingPolicy, L39, which never unloads the currently serving version until its successor is fully ready.
  • Finally, the request path: PredictionServiceImpl::Predict, L38 receives the gRPC call, acquires a scoped ServableHandle, L75 through Manager::GetUntypedServableHandle, L109, and executes the signature via the predictor in TensorflowPredictor::Predict, L33.

Inside the Loading Flow

The overview deliberately hides the most interesting machinery: what exactly happens between “a new version directory appeared” and “requests now flow to it”. The detail diagram expands that seam, and it is where the design earns its reputation.

The detailed view: adapter wiring, the manager and its policies, per-servable harnesses, state monitoring, and the batching layer wrapped around the session.

Start with the adapter contract. Everything that feeds models into the manager is a Source, L65 — a thing that pushes aspired versions to a callback. A SourceAdapter, L60 is a source that transforms another source’s output, and the storage-path-to-SavedModel chain is exactly two such hops: the file system source emits StoragePath items, an adapter turns them into loadable servables. ServerCore::CreateRouter, L696 inserts a dynamic router between them so each model name reaches only its own adapter.

Inside the manager, every candidate version is wrapped in a LoaderHarness, L52, a tiny state machine that moves each servable through new, loading, ready, and unloading states while guarding transitions against races. The harness drives a Loader, L57, whose Load() at Load, L90 materializes the model. Crucially, Loader::EstimateResources() lets the manager decide whether the new version even fits before starting the load; the estimate comes from EstimateResourceFromPath, L92 in the SavedModel case. BasicManager, L106 implements the thread pools and retry logic behind AspiredVersionsManager, L85, and both report every state change to a ServableStateMonitor, L46, which is what powers the model-status API implemented in GetModelStatusImpl::GetModelStatus, L66.

The batching layer is similarly clean. When you pass --enable_batching, the factory does not wrap the raw session; it wraps it once at load time using WrapSessionForBatching, L100, so every request for that model transparently goes through BatchingSession. That class queues incoming runs into a StreamingBatchScheduler, L114, merges tensors with the padding helpers in batching_util, executes one combined Session::Run, then splits outputs back per request in ProcessBatch, L717. Because batching is a session decorator rather than a server feature, it composes with any platform that exposes a session-shaped interface.

Step back and the pattern across all of this is dependency injection with interfaces, done the C++ way: sources produce, adapters transform, loaders own, and the manager schedules. No component above knows about HTTP or protobufs, which is why the same core has survived years of runtime churn underneath it. When you next evaluate a serving system, ask whether it can express “keep serving 6 until 7 is ready, but never if both cannot fit in memory” as a first-class rule — here it is roughly one policy class plus one estimate function.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path is Docker: docker pull tensorflow/serving, then run the container with --model_base_path=/models/my_model mounted from the host. The image listens on 8500 for gRPC and 8501 for REST by default. If you prefer packages on Ubuntu, a one-line apt-get install tensorflow-model-server from the project’s repository works, and a plain pip install tensorflow-serving-api gives you the generated Python clients for both APIs.

Preparing a model means exporting a SavedModel with a numbered version directory: /models/my_model/123/ containing saved_model.pb and a variables/ folder. Point --model_base_path at /models/my_model — the parent, never the version directory — and the server picks the highest number by default. Restarting to deploy is optional: with --model_config_file you can serve many models from one process, and with --model_config_file_poll_wait_seconds the server re-reads that config periodically, so adding a model is a file edit rather than a restart.

Two flags are worth enabling on day one. --enable_batching activates the batching session described above, tunable through --batching_parameters_file where you set max batch size, timeout in microseconds, and the number of threads; without it, every request runs alone. --enable_model_warmup triggers the warmup replay so lazy initializations happen during load instead of on your first customer request. For an HTTP smoke test, curl -d '{"instances":[[1.0,2.0,5.0]]}' -X POST http://localhost:8501/v1/models/my_model:predict is usually the first thing people run — note the REST handler behind that URL lives in HttpRestApiHandler, L56, dispatched by the embedded server in http_server.cc. For training the model you will deploy, our earlier TensorFlow overview covers the export side, and if you need to serve non-TensorFlow formats, the adapters in this repository stop at TF-style inputs — that is where the alternatives come in.

Honest Limits

TensorFlow Serving is battle-tested, but it is opinionated, and several of its opinions will cost you. The biggest one: it serves TensorFlow formats. A PyTorch or ONNX artifact must be converted first, and some conversions are lossy; if your stack is not TensorFlow-native, Triton Server or TorchServe will save you a translation layer. Second, the served-model surface is static by design — the binary serves a configured set of models and version directories, and there is no built-in dynamic model registry, no authentication layer, and no rate limiting. You are expected to put a proxy in front and handle auth outside the process.

Third, memory behavior during swaps deserves respect. With the default availability-preserving policy, old and new versions coexist in RAM until the new one is warm, so a redeploy of a 30 GB model briefly needs twice that; the alternative ResourcePreservingPolicy, L42 unloads first but risks a serving gap. Fourth, batching defaults are conservative and single-model scoped; per-model tuning requires either the config file or the newer per-model batching_params.pbtxt dropped into the SavedModel directory. Fifth, contributing is not casual: the build is Bazel, the tests are extensive, and the abstractions are template-heavy C++, so most teams treat the binary as a product rather than a library. None of these are disqualifying — they are the price of a server that has handled production inference at enormous scale for most of a decade. Read the interfaces once, and every flag in main.cc becomes an obvious knob.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the TensorFlow Serving C++ codebase: how SavedModels are discovered on disk, versioned, loaded, batched, and answered over gRPC and REST.

entry.title: WhisperX: Batched Whisper, wav2vec2 Alignment and Diarization From the Source Up

link.title: WhisperX: Batched Whisper, wav2vec2 Alignment and Diarization From the Source Up

entry.content:
WhisperX is one of those repositories that looks small from the outside — a Python package and a CLI called whisperx — but underneath it coordinates three very different machine learning models against the same audio buffer. A faster-whisper CTranslate2 engine does the speech recognition, a wav2vec2 phoneme model anchors every word to an exact time range, and a pyannote speaker model answers the “who spoke when” question. The reason people reach for it is simple: vanilla Whisper decodes audio sequentially and its timestamps are only segment-accurate, while WhisperX batches the decoding and then recovers word-level timestamps with a second, cheaper model.

Reading the source matters because the interesting engineering is in the handoffs. Voice activity detection decides where speech actually is, those regions get packed into up-to-30-second chunks, the chunks fly through the recognizer in parallel batches, and only then does the aligner see the transcript. If you have ever wondered why your transcription tool hallucinates on silence or drops words at chunk boundaries, the answers are in this code. The design also explains WhisperX’s memory discipline: each stage explicitly unloads its model and calls gc.collect() before the next one loads, so a laptop GPU can survive the whole sequence.

This post walks the repository the way we have been touring other inference projects — Piper for on-device TTS, ONNX Runtime for portable model execution — except here the subject is speech recognition, and the tour ends at subtitle files rather than audio. Two diagrams were generated directly from the repository tree: a compact overview and a detailed call-level map. Every symbol mentioned below links to the real line in the upstream source on main.

Architecture at a Glance

From CLI entry through voice activity, batched recognition, alignment and speaker labeling to the output writers.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The journey starts at cli, L12, which builds the entire argparse surface — model size, device, compute type, VAD thresholds, diarization flags — and dispatches into the task function.
  • load_audio, L25 decodes any container format through ffmpeg into 16 kHz mono float32, and the module-level SAMPLE_RATE, L13 constant is the contract every later stage relies on.
  • load_model, L462 is the factory that wires the faster-whisper engine, tokenizer defaults and one of the two VAD backends into a single object.
  • The Vad, L7 base class defines the backend contract, and its static merge_chunks, L20 helper packs detected speech regions into batchable chunks.
  • Two backends implement that contract: load_vad_model, L21 for the default pyannote route and Silero, L18 for the lightweight alternative.
  • transcribe, L257 is where batching happens: chunks become a DataLoader, and each batch is encoded and decoded in parallel on the GPU.
  • align, L152 then runs wav2vec2 forced alignment over the same waveform to pin words to milliseconds.
  • When --diarize is passed, assign_word_speakers, L185 overlaps those words with pyannote speaker turns.
  • Finally get_writer, L443 selects the output format — srt, vtt, tsv, json, txt or Audacity labels.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one line, plus ffmpeg on your PATH:

pip install whisperx

Then the CLI does the whole sequence in one shot:

whisperx audio.mp3 --model large-v2 --batch_size 16 \
  --compute_type float16 --diarize --hf_token YOUR_HF_TOKEN \
  --output_format all

Three flags deserve attention. --batch_size controls how many VAD chunks are decoded in parallel — this is the main speed lever, and raising it is safe precisely because chunks are independent. --vad_method switches between pyannote (default) and silero; the code in load_model treats a manually supplied VAD model as higher priority than the method flag. --diarize pulls in a gated pyannote model, which is why an HF token is needed.

The same sequence works as a library, which is what most production code should use:

import whisperx, gc

device = "cuda"
model = whisperx.load_model("large-v2", device, compute_type="float16")
audio = whisperx.load_audio("audio.mp3")
result = model.transcribe(audio, batch_size=16)
del model; gc.collect()          # free Whisper before loading the aligner

align_model, meta = whisperx.load_align_model(result["language"], device)
result = whisperx.align(result["segments"], align_model, meta, audio, device)

The Python surface mirrors the CLI’s three stages exactly, and that mirrors the internal call graph: load_model returns the engine wrapper, transcribe returns a plain dict matching the TranscriptionResult, L65 TypedDict, and align upgrades it in place to the aligned shape. Note the explicit del and gc.collect() between stages — when you orchestrate the models yourself, the memory handoff is your responsibility, not the library’s. The package/__init__.py exports only the handful of names above, which is a quiet design statement: the intended composition is short, and anything fancier should go through the CLI.

What comes back depends on the format. The JSON dump mirrors the AlignedTranscriptionResult, L73 TypedDict — segments, and inside each one a words array where every entry carries start, end, word and, after diarization, speaker. The srt and vtt files are rendered from the same structure by the subtitle writer, which is why word-level highlighting works there too.

Under the hood the engine class extends faster_whisper.WhisperModel directly (see WhisperModel, L32), so anything CTranslate2 supports — float16 on CUDA, float32 on CPU, int8 quantization via --compute_type — carries over unchanged.

The Batched Inference Loop

The detailed map: VAD chunking feeds a DataLoader-style iterator, whose batches flow through encode and batched beam-search decode, then onward to alignment and diarization.

The heart of the repo is what happens inside transcribe, L257. First the VAD backend runs over the waveform; its onset and offset thresholds (defaults 0.500 and 0.363, tunable via --vad_onset/--vad_offset) decide what counts as speech. The detected regions are then merged by merge_chunks into windows of at most chunk_size seconds — 30 by default. Crucially, the code checks the backend with issubclass(type(self.vad_model), Vad) and falls back to the pyannote preprocessing path otherwise, which is what lets you plug in a custom VAD.

Those chunks feed get_iterator, L236, a torch DataLoader over slice indices computed with SAMPLE_RATE arithmetic, so workers pull raw audio slices lazily instead of copying the whole buffer. Each batch goes through encode, L121, which pads log-mel features into a CTranslate2 StorageView, and lands in generate_segment_batched, L38 for batched beam-search decoding. If you never passed --language, detect_language, L447 runs once per file as a fallback and the tokenizer is built from the answer.

One subtlety worth stealing: when --suppress_numerals is set, the decoder suppresses numeric tokens (the helper lives at the top of asr.py). Why? Because wav2vec2 phoneme models are bad at aligning digits — “2026” spoken aloud has no written form to match — so WhisperX prefers spelled-out text it can align faithfully, and later stages fix the rendering.

The stage boundaries are also where memory gets reclaimed. After the last file is transcribed, the code deletes the ASR object, calls gc.collect() and empties the CUDA cache before loading the alignment model. Same after alignment, before diarization. It reads like ceremony, but on a 6 GB GPU it is the difference between finishing and OOM.

wav2vec2 Forced Alignment, Then Speaker Labels

Alignment is where WhisperX earns its name. The DEFAULT_ALIGN_MODELS_HF, L71 registry maps each language to a wav2vec2-style phoneme checkpoint (English gets a wav2vec2 model; Japanese and Chinese, which lack spaces, live in a separate constant and use different word-joining rules). load_align_model, L111 fetches the right one — and if the transcript’s language differs from the aligner’s, the CLI reloads a matching aligner mid-run.

The algorithm inside align, L152 is a textbook Viterbi forced alignment: run the wav2vec2 model over the audio to get per-frame phoneme probabilities, build a frame-by-token trellis with get_trellis, L548, recover the best path with backtrack, L574, collapse repeated tokens into spans with merge_repeats, L625, and join spans into words with merge_words, L643. Words the aligner could not place get NaN timestamps, which interpolate_nans, L470 fills by nearest or linear interpolation depending on --interpolate_method.

Diarization is deliberately thin. The wrapper in diarize.py loads a pyannote speaker model (community release 1 is the current default name in the CLI), runs it over the file, and returns turn annotations as Segment, L266 objects — start, end, speaker. assign_word_speakers, L185 then indexes those turns and walks every aligned word through an IntervalTree, L14 to find which turn overlaps it most; the winning speaker label is written onto the word and majority-voted upward to the parent segment. No embeddings dance unless you ask for --speaker_embeddings.

Honest Limits

The alignment chain inherits wav2vec2’s weaknesses. Digits, acronyms and code-switched speech align poorly — hence the numeral suppression trick — and exotic languages fall back to multilingual checkpoints with noticeably sloppier boundaries. If no per-language aligner exists, --no_align degrades you back to segment-level timestamps.

VAD is a hard gate, not a suggestion. Music-heavy or overlapping-speech audio produces merged or missing chunks, and everything downstream inherits that blindness. The chunking heuristic (30 seconds, onset/offset thresholds) is tuned for speech-dominant audio; long-form noisy recordings deserve their own threshold sweep. Whisper processes audio in fixed 30-second windows regardless of content, which is exactly why the VAD-first design is faster — but it also means a bad VAD run poisons the whole batch. Upstream offers two soft mitigations inside the decoder: --hotwords biases recognition toward rare or technical terms you expect in the audio, and --interleaved_context re-runs the first batch of streams with wrap-around context so chunk boundaries see their neighbors’ tokens.

Diarization needs that HF token and downloads a gated pyannote checkpoint on first run; offline deployments must pre-cache it. And while the batched decoder is dramatically faster than sequential decoding, batch_size is bounded by VRAM: 16 GB comfortably handles large-v2 at batch 16 in float16, less does not.

For readers comparing engines: the batching philosophy here rhymes with what FasterTransformer did for transformer serving, while the model-to-runtime split (CTranslate2 for Whisper, HF transformers auto model loading for wav2vec2, pyannote for speakers) is a reminder that production speech systems are rarely one framework — much like Transformers serves as the common loader layer across the ecosystem. WhisperX’s real lesson is architectural: keep each model in its lane, pass one canonical buffer, and spend your complexity budget on the handoffs.
entry.summary: A source tour of m-bain/whisperX: how faster-whisper batched inference, wav2vec2 forced alignment and pyannote speaker diarization hand off one 16 kHz buffer from CLI entry to subtitle writers.
